newsitem.title: MEXICO: Ford de Mexico output off due to work stoppages.
newsitem.headline: Ford de Mexico output off due to work stoppages.

text.p: Ford de Mexico, a subsidiary of Ford Motor Co, has lost production of about 1,300 vehicles and 2,000 motors because of work stoppages at its three Mexican plants, a company spokesman said on Wednesday.

Workers were still idled on Wednesday at Ford's Cuautitlan assembly plant just north of Mexico City after walking off the job on Monday, Ford spokesman Carlos Hernandez said. But the Hermosillo assembly plant and the Chihuahua motor plant in northern Mexico were back to work after temporary stoppages, he said.

Hernandez said the workers walked off the job in protest after the company said on Friday it would not offer profit-sharing bonuses this year because Ford de Mexico lost 1.657 billion pesos, about $207 million, in 1996.
"Because of this situation (the losses), there won't be profit-sharing, and the workers were not in agreement," Hernandez told Reuters.

Company and union officials met on Tuesday night at the Labor Ministry in Mexico City but failed to reach an agreement, a union leader said. The two sides were scheduled to meet again under Labor Ministry mediation on Wednesday.

"We are going to stop work again if there is no economic compensation for profits," Ariel Burgos, the union leader at the Hermosillo plant, told Reuters by telephone. "On Friday we're are going to have a general assembly to determine what we will do."

Hernandez said workers at the Hermosillo plant walked off the job on Friday afternoon and stayed out all day on Monday, costing the plant about 1,000 units of production of its Ford Escort and Mercury Tracer models, primarily for export to the United States and Canada. Hermosillo workers returned to work on Tuesday, he said.

In Chihuahua, workers walked off the job to start the second shift on Monday and held out Tuesday but returned to work on Wednesday, Hernandez said. The company lost production of about 2,000 motors for the export and domestic markets.

At Cuautitlan, a smaller plant primarily for the domestic market, workers walked off the job on Monday afternoon and all day Tuesday, idling production of about 300 units, Hernandez said. They still had not returned to work on Wednesday morning.

Hernandez said the workers did not understand how Ford de Mexico could be losing money while improving its position in the Mexican market. From 1994 to 1996, Ford increased its market share in Mexico from 15 percent to 20 percent, moving from fifth place in the market to second place.

Despite hard times in recent years because of Mexico's deep recesion, the company has always paid profit-sharing -- eight percent of after-tax profits -- or a small bonus to workers if there were no profits, Hernandez said. The company decided not to pay a bonus this year because of accumulated losses.
"(The company) keeps saying that it has improved its situation but that now there are losses," said Burgos, the union leader. "It's not logical."
